comparability.reason: Study provides correlations between naturally varying matrix constituents (pH, ammonia) and PFAS removal in a single field system without controlled side-by-side clean-water conditions or fixed influent PFAS concentrations; removal endpoints are influenced by uncontrolled seasonal changes, limiting quantitative comparability with controlled lab studies.

endpoints.interpretation: Total, short-chain, and long-chain PFAS removal efficiencies by CPS and ZIPGEM were evaluated under varying field water quality (pH, ammonia, season). PFAS removal was used as the performance metric for the filtration cells.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS removal efficiency

endpoints.interpretation: Spearman and PCA analyses showed that total PFAS removal efficiency is negatively associated with influent and effluent ammonia concentrations; PFOS removal appeared most impacted, with PFAS removal loading in a quadrant opposite to ammonia in PCA space, indicating ammonia-related competition or charge effects on adsorption.
endpoints.reported_term: Effect of ammonia on PFAS removal efficiency

endpoints.interpretation: Short- and long-chain PFAS removal efficiencies were negatively correlated with proton concentration (i.e., decreased when pH decreased). Short-chain PFAS showed stronger negative correlation, consistent with electrostatic adsorption sensitivity to surface protonation and charge neutralization, whereas long-chain PFAS, dominated by hydrophobic interactions, were less affected.
endpoints.reported_term: Effect of pH (proton concentration) on PFAS removal

endpoints.interpretation: Authors infer that proton exchange among DOC, ammonium ions, and media components, driven by changes in influent/effluent pH, affects media surface charge and hence PFAS removal. Increased NH4+ in the media over time, formation of ammonium at lower pH, and protonation/deprotonation of media and natural organic matter are proposed to influence PFAS adsorption via competition, charge neutralization, and changes in cation-bridging capacity.
endpoints.reported_term: Water-matrix interaction mechanisms (ammonia, DOM, protons)

limitations.statement: PFAS removal efficiencies and inferred water-matrix effects are based on a single field canal source with seasonally varying composition, without a clean-water (synthetic matrix) control for direct comparison.

Influent and effluent ammonia measurements do not directly quantify NH4+ concentration within the media bed, so interpretations of competitive effects and charge interactions rely on indirect evidence (e.g., effluent ammonia increases over time).

record.citation: Ika, A.R.; Lin, S.F.; Wang, C.L.; Chang-Chien, G.P.; Huang, B.W. Occurrence, partitioning, and fate of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in a full-scale AO-MBR-RO municipal WWTP. J. Water Process Eng. 2025, 80, 109196.

comparability.reason: Field observations in a single full-scale AO–MBR–RO WWTP with inherently variable municipal wastewater matrix and no paired clean-water controls; results characterize real-matrix partitioning and redistribution rather than controlled matrix effects and are thus more suitable for qualitative insights than direct quantitative comparison across treatment technologies or matrices.

endpoints.interpretation: Stage-wise PFAS reduction was evaluated by comparing concentrations and daily mass loads across AO, MBR, and RO units. The MBR achieved partial ΣPFAS reduction (~61%), while RO achieved high PFAS rejection (>94% from feed to permeate) but concentrated PFAS in brine rather than destroying them.
endpoints.reported_term: removal efficiency and reduction

endpoints.interpretation: RO performance was assessed as separation/rejection of PFAS from the aqueous phase into the brine. Compound-specific partitioning between aqueous streams and sludge was quantified, showing preferential accumulation of PFOS and long-chain PFCAs in sludge and continued mobility of short-chain and emerging PFAS in aqueous phases.
endpoints.reported_term: rejection and partitioning

endpoints.interpretation: Concentration changes of individual PFAS across stages (e.g., PFOS, PF4OPeA) were tracked. AO mobilized matrix-bound PFAS and likely transformed precursors, leading to apparent increases in terminal PFAS (e.g., PFOS spikes post-AO, PF4OPeA increases after primary sedimentation) rather than true destruction.
endpoints.reported_term: concentration changes and apparent increases

endpoints.interpretation: Authors hypothesized in-situ precursor transformation, particularly of sulfonamides and ether-type PFAS, during biological treatment and anaerobic digestion, contributing to increased loads of terminal PFAS such as PFOS and other PFAAs. Transformation was inferred from load increases rather than direct precursor quantification in the provided excerpts.
endpoints.reported_term: precursor transformation

endpoints.interpretation: Mass-balance analysis of daily PFAS loads across aqueous and sludge streams showed that the AO–MBR–RO system largely redistributed PFAS between effluent, RO brine, and biosolids rather than eliminating them, with ~89% of influent PFAS mass appearing in final effluent and 159% in sludge, indicating net enrichment via matrix concentration and precursor conversion.
endpoints.reported_term: mass balance and fate

limitations.statement: The study evaluates a single full-scale AO–MBR–RO municipal WWTP with complex, variable influent; results may not be directly generalizable to different plant configurations or cleaner water matrices.
Transformation of PFAS precursors is inferred from increases in terminal PFAS loads rather than directly quantified precursor concentrations or transformation products in the provided excerpts.
